Why is selling a house in New York City different from selling elsewhere?

The city is five boroughs and five counties, so the recording office and paperwork depend on where the house stands. Manhattan is New York County, Brooklyn is Kings County, Queens and the Bronx share names with their counties, and Staten Island is Richmond County.

The Department of Finance sorts every property into one of four tax classes by use. A house of up to three units falls in Class 1, and co-ops and most condominiums go in Class 2. The city also runs its own transfer tax. This page concentrates on houses rather than co-op shares.

For July 1, 2025 the Census Bureau estimates 8,584,629 residents, down 2.5 percent from the 2020 base, packed at 29,303 people per square mile over about 300 square miles of land.

How do the boroughs differ for someone with a house to sell?

Staten Island is the most suburban and calls itself the Borough of Parks, with about 12,300 acres of protected parkland. The Bronx is the only borough on the mainland and holds Pelham Bay Park, the city's largest at 2,772 acres. Queens is the biggest by area and has JFK and LaGuardia airports within its lines.

Brooklyn has the most residents and a long beachfront that includes Coney Island. Manhattan is the smallest and densest borough, at more than 70,000 people per square mile.

  • Staten Island: Richmond County, tied to Brooklyn by the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and to Manhattan by a free ferry
  • The Bronx: home to Co-op City, the largest cooperatively owned housing complex in the country
  • Queens: on Long Island, north and east of Brooklyn
  • Brooklyn: at the western tip of Long Island

How many New Yorkers own their homes?

Fewer than a third do. The 2020 to 2024 Census figures show owners in 32.8 percent of households, a typical owned-home value of $777,600 and a typical rent of $1,821.

That leaves a renter-heavy city where houses are a modest slice. The city has 3,334,088 households of about 2.48 people each, with a median household income of $80,483 in 2024 dollars. Foreign-born residents are 36.6 percent of the population, and 47.7 percent of people over four speak another language at home.

Workers spend 40.3 minutes getting to their jobs, the longest figure among the four places in this Census comparison. If your house sits near a subway stop or commuter rail line, lead the listing with that.

How is property tax calculated and billed on a New York City house?

The tax year runs from July 1 to June 30, and each property is billed by tax class and assessed value. A property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed four times a year, and one above that is billed twice.

Tax classWhat it coversRate for tax year 2026
Class 1Most residential property of up to three units19.843%
Class 2Other primarily residential property, such as co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Property with gas, telephone or electric company equipment11.108%
Class 4All other property, such as offices and warehouses10.848%

Source: NYC Department of Finance property tax rates and glossary pages.

Quarterly bills come due on the first of July, October, January and April, each with a grace period to the 15th. Twice-a-year bills fall on July 1 and January 1. Settling the whole year by the July due date earns a 0.50 percent discount, and interest on late balances compounds daily. If a bill is still open when you sell, ask your closing attorney how it will be handled at closing.

When must a house owner contest an assessment in New York City?

The NYC Tax Commission, an independent agency, takes the appeal, and a Class 1 owner must file by March 15. Classes 2, 3 and 4 face March 1, and late filings are denied. The Commission can lower an assessment, change the tax class and adjust exemptions.

Finance has a separate track: a Request for Review to correct a description or clerical slip, due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other classes. It does not replace an appeal, so file both when both apply.

Owners of high-value homes that are not their primary residence face a newer charge. A law effective May 28, 2026 adds a surcharge of 0.8 percent of market value on one, two and three-family houses worth $5 million or more, climbing to 1.05 and 1.3 percent at higher values. A house used as a primary residence by the owner, a tenant or a relative is exempt. The 2026-27 exemption deadline was October 13, 2026, and any charge shows on the bill due January 1, 2027.

What comes out of the sale price at a New York City closing?

Several layers apply. The seller owes the state's base tax of $2 per $500 of price, and the city adds its own real property transfer tax, normally settled with the other closing costs. For residential conveyances at $3 million or more, the state tacks on a further $1.25 per $500, also on the seller.

The buyer's side has the mansion tax at 1 percent from $1 million up, plus a supplemental tax between 0.25 and 2.9 percent once a residential price reaches $2 million. The city return, Form NYC-RPT, is created online in ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Both parties sign it, and a late return adds 5 percent of the tax per month, capped at 25 percent.

Your attorney can quote the exact city figure, which varies with the kind of transfer and the price. A seller living outside New York State must work out the gain and pay any estimated income tax unless an exemption on Form TP-584-NYC applies.

What does a certificate of occupancy have to do with a New York City sale?

The certificate states the legal use of a building, and nobody may lawfully occupy a structure until the Department of Buildings issues either a final certificate or a temporary one (TCO). A final certificate never expires, but the Department will not issue one while the property has open applications or open violations.

To obtain a final certificate, the Department requires:

  • Final construction, plumbing, elevator and electrical inspection sign-offs
  • A final building survey and an Owner's Cost Affidavit
  • No open applications and no open violations

Buildings put up before 1938 may not need one. A Letter of No Objection from the borough office can document their legal use. Search your address in DOB NOW to see whether a certificate is on file.

The Department urges buyers to close on a final certificate, since an expired and unrenewed TCO can make a house hard to insure, sell or refinance. If you finished a basement or built an extension without closing out the job, a cash buyer taking the house as-is will price that in, so resolve or disclose it before accepting an offer.

More questions about New York, NY

On what dates do New York City property tax bills come due?

July 1 and January 1 for twice-a-year payers. Quarterly payers also owe on October 1 and April 1, with a grace period running to the 15th.

What is the 2026 tax rate for a one-family house in the city?

The Department of Finance sets the Class 1 rate at 19.843 percent. Class 1 covers most residential property of up to three units, so a one-family house falls in it.

How long do I have to appeal my house assessment?

Until March 15 for Class 1, filed with the NYC Tax Commission. Owners of Class 2, 3 and 4 property must file by March 1.

Who bears the state transfer tax in a city sale?

The seller pays the base $2 per $500 unless the contract says otherwise. The buyer pays the mansion tax when the price is $1 million or more.

Is a certificate of occupancy required to sell?

Not always. A house built before 1938 may lack one, and a Letter of No Objection from the Department of Buildings can show its legal use. For anything newer or altered, expect the buyer's attorney to ask.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Islip at a glance

  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 340,867 (Census Bureau).
  • Islip is in Suffolk County.
Selling in Islip?
We buy Islip houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Taxes on the sale itself

See the transfer tax guide.

What does selling a house in Islip, NY involve?

Selling a house in the Town of Islip means choosing between a listing with an agent, a sale you manage yourself, or an offer from a cash buyer, then closing through a deed recorded with the Suffolk County Clerk. The town is large, so the details change from one hamlet to the next, but the paperwork path is the same everywhere inside its borders.

Mid-2025 Census estimates give Islip 340,867 people, up 0.3% from the 2020 base. Its 2020-2024 survey shows 102,205 households and 3.28 people per household, so the typical Islip household is large. When one of those homes comes to market because of an inheritance, a move or a debt problem, the owner usually needs to settle three things: what the house needs before it can close, what taxes and fees come out of the proceeds, and how fast the money is needed.

  • List with an agent if the home shows well and you can wait through showings and a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Sell it yourself only if you are comfortable handling the contract, disclosure and attorney review without a broker.
  • Take a cash offer when speed, an as-is condition or a difficult title or occupancy situation matters more than the top price.

Where is Islip and what does the layout mean for a seller?

Islip is a South Shore town in Suffolk County, bounded by the Atlantic Ocean to the south, Babylon to the west, Smithtown to the north and Brookhaven to the east. Its total area is about 162.8 square miles, but only 103.2 of those are land, because the Great South Bay and the barrier islands make up the rest.

Islip dates to 1683, when land was bought from the sachem of Connetquot. The original grant reached from East Islip to Bayport and took in Sayville, West Sayville, Oakdale, Great River, Islip Terrace, Central Islip, Hauppauge, Holbrook, Bohemia, Brentwood, Holtsville and part of Ronkonkoma. Bay Shore and West Islip were also early patents. Today the town runs through at least 17 ZIP codes, and a buyer shopping for a house in Sayville is looking at a different market than one shopping in Brentwood or Hauppauge.

The town also holds part of Fire Island, Jones Beach Island and Captree Island. A house on the bay side of the mainland or near the barrier islands raises insurance and flood-zone questions that an inland house in Hauppauge does not, so a seller should pull the flood and survey paperwork early. Roads that frame the town include Route 231 near the Babylon line, the Long Island Expressway to the north and Nicolls Road toward Brookhaven, according to the town's geography on Wikipedia.

How does home ownership look across the Town of Islip?

Islip is mostly a town of owners: 80.5% of housing units are owner-occupied, and the middle owned home in the 2020-2024 survey is valued at $535,300. Median household income over the same period is $130,132, and the average commute takes 28.3 minutes.

Monthly owner costs matter to a seller weighing a quick exit. The median with a mortgage is $3,222 a month, and the median gross rent is $2,209. A homeowner who is behind on payments or carrying a second property can see why holding on costs more each month than many people expect. One more figure: 92.7% of residents had not moved in the prior twelve months, so most owners stay put and a sale usually follows a life event.

The same survey shows 32.6% of adults with a four-year degree and a poverty rate of 6.4%. Those numbers say Islip is not one uniform market. A town of this size has many price levels, so ask an appraiser or agent for recent sales on your own street rather than relying on a town-wide figure.

What does the Town of Islip Building Division handle when a house sells?

The Building Division, at One Manitton Court in Islip, issues permits and closes them out with a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance, and that paperwork often decides whether a sale closes smoothly. The Records Office schedules inspections and handles requests for building department records, including surveys, permits, certificates of occupancy, building plans and inspection reports.

If you finished a basement, added a deck or converted a garage, check that the permit was closed. Open or missing permits tend to surface when a buyer's attorney orders a records search. The division takes records requests through its online Freedom of Information form, and the Records Office line is 631-224-5470. The front counter closes at 4:00 pm on weekdays.

  • Permit applications must be filed electronically, and the division asks applicants to follow its Electronic Submittal Process flyer.
  • Inspections are scheduled through the Records Office, because inspectors cannot book them directly.
  • An updated NYS Uniform Code and State Energy Code took effect on December 31, 2025, so permit applications accepted after that date are reviewed under the newer rules.

The Town of Islip also publishes a Map Viewer that shows the zoning district of a property, which helps when a buyer asks whether a second kitchen or accessory unit is allowed.

What will recording an Islip sale with the Suffolk County Clerk run?

A deed for an Islip property is recorded with the Suffolk County Clerk, and the clerk lists the base deed charge as $245 plus $5 per page, with transfer tax charged separately. Your attorney or title company normally prepares the package and pays at closing, but knowing the line items helps you read a settlement statement.

ItemAmount or ruleSource
Suffolk deed recording charge$245 plus $5 per pageSuffolk County Clerk deed fee schedule
New York State transfer tax$2 per $500 of consideration, or fraction, when the price exceeds $500Suffolk County Clerk and NYS Tax Department
Mansion tax1% on residential sales of $1,000,000 or more, paid by the buyerSuffolk County Clerk and NYS Tax Department
Transfer tax payment deadlineWithin 15 days of delivering the deedNYS Tax Department

The seller bears the state transfer tax, and the buyer picks it up only when the seller is exempt or leaves it unpaid. On a $535,300 sale, the Census median home value, the tax works out to $2,142 under the $2 per $500 formula. The Peconic Bay Region Community Preservation form is needed only for the five East End towns, which do not include Islip. A seller who lives outside New York may need form IT-2663 filed with the deed. Checks for recording fees go to the Suffolk County Clerk, and its main line is (631) 852-2000.

How do weather and flooding affect selling in Islip?

Water is the main weather issue for Islip sellers, because the town sits low and faces the Atlantic. The town's listed elevation is 6.6 feet, and the climate record at Long Island MacArthur Airport shows annual precipitation of 45.99 inches, spread fairly evenly through the months, with March and December the wettest.

On August 12 and 13, 2014, a 24-hour rainfall of 13.57 inches set a New York State record, including 1.08 inches in nine minutes, and flooded the Southern State Parkway and Sunrise Highway. A buyer's inspector will ask about past water in basements and crawl spaces, so keep repair receipts and any insurance claims together. Snowfall averages 31.8 inches a year, falling mostly from November to April, so roof and gutter condition are routine inspection items.

Summer heat is modest, with a July daily mean of 75.0 degrees Fahrenheit, and winters average 31.9 degrees in January.

When does a cash offer fit an Islip house?

A cash offer fits when the house needs work, carries a title or tenant complication, or must sell on a short timeline. It does not fit every Islip homeowner, and a well-kept house in a strong hamlet may net more on the open market.

Compare the offer against a realistic listing outcome, after subtracting agent commission, repairs, carrying costs and the months of waiting. Get the figures on paper, confirm who pays the transfer tax and recording costs, and have a New York attorney review the contract before you sign. Check whether the buyer will close with an existing open permit or missing certificate of occupancy, since that is where an as-is sale in Islip most often changes the numbers.

  • Inherited houses where several heirs need to agree and the estate needs liquid cash.
  • Houses with deferred repairs, storm damage or open building permits.
  • Owners facing a move, a divorce or a mortgage default who need a firm closing date.

More questions about Islip, NY

Is the state transfer tax my bill when I sell in Islip?

The seller pays it. The state rate is $2 per $500 of the sale price, and the buyer picks it up only when the seller is exempt or leaves it unpaid. The deadline is 15 days from delivery of the deed, and the Suffolk County Clerk collects it at recording.

Where is a deed for an Islip house recorded?

The Suffolk County Clerk records it, and the office insists on original signatures, a notary acknowledgment, full names and street addresses for all parties, and a legal description that names the village, town, county and state. Post office boxes are not accepted as addresses.

Can I sell an Islip house that has an open building permit?

Yes, though a title search or the buyer's attorney will likely flag it. Ask the Building Division Records Office whether the permit can be closed with a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance, and use the town's online records request to pull the file.

What is the population of the Town of Islip?

The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 340,867 residents, compared with 339,938 in the 2020 census. About 103 square miles of the town is land, and the 2020 density was 3,294 people per square mile.

Does the Peconic Bay form apply to a sale in Islip?

No. The Suffolk County Clerk requires that form only for deeds in Riverhead, Southampton, East Hampton, Shelter Island and Southold. Islip sellers still need the RP-5217 transfer report and the TP-584 transfer tax return with the deed.

Buffalo at a glance

  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 274,613 (Census Bureau).
  • Buffalo is in Erie County.
Selling in Buffalo?
We buy Buffalo houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Taxes on the sale itself

See the transfer tax guide.

How can I sell my house fast in Buffalo, NY?

Three paths exist: an agent listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale, or a direct purchase by a company like ours. The direct purchase moves fastest because no lender has to sign off on the buyer. Condition usually decides it. A worn two-family with deferred repairs, or a rental that failed the city's inspection, drags on a listing, while an investor can price the same house as it stands.

Renters outnumber owners in Buffalo. Only 43.0% of homes house the person who owns them (Census Bureau, 2020-2024), which means much of the stock is income property that must satisfy city registration rules before it can legally collect rent.

How do Buffalo's housing figures compare?

The Census Bureau estimates 274,613 people lived in Buffalo on July 1, 2025, a 1.3% drop since April 2020. The figures below show why a repair bill can swallow a large share of a sale price here.

Buffalo measure (Census Bureau QuickFacts)Figure
Residents, April 1, 2020 census278,349
Land area40.38 square miles
Households, 2020-2024119,630
Homes where the owner lives43.0%
Median value of an owner's home$164,200
Median gross rent$1,046
Median household income$50,041

Against a $164,200 median, a $25,000 roof or porch rebuild takes a meaningful bite out of a house's worth, and a buyer will subtract it from any bid. Median gross rent is $1,046 a month, so an investor who plans to rent the house out works backward from that figure, and a unit that cannot yet pass inspection has to be priced lower to account for the repair bill.

Where is Buffalo and how did it become a city?

Buffalo sits on the eastern shore of Lake Erie at the head of the Niagara River and is the seat of Erie County. Wikipedia gives its area as 52.48 square miles, of which 40.38 is land and 12.10 is water.

The land around Buffalo Creek passed through the Holland Land Purchase, and Buffalo was chosen as the terminus of the Erie Canal in 1825. The city charter followed in 1832, and Buffalo became a major grain port, then the second-largest railway hub in the country after Chicago, and later a steel town. Deindustrialization and the St. Lawrence Seaway pulled that economy apart, and the city has since leaned on health care, education, retail, logistics and tourism.

Which Buffalo neighborhoods and roads matter to a buyer?

Wikipedia notes that Buffalo's West Side is generally more affluent than its East Side, and that investment has gathered in a handful of districts since the 1990s. A house's address can move its value as much as its condition does.

  • Elmwood Village led the wave of reinvestment that began in the 1990s.
  • Larkinville grew out of the 2002 redevelopment of the Larkin Terminal Warehouse.
  • Downtown added more than 1,000 housing units between 2010 and 2017, and Seneca One Tower was redeveloped in 2020.
  • The Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus covers about 120 acres north of downtown.

I-190, NY 5 and NY 33 are the main expressways, and the Peace Bridge links I-190 to Canada. NFTA Metro Rail runs 6.4 miles from Canalside to the University Heights district. Buffalo Public Schools enroll roughly 34,000 students in about 60 schools, and the University at Buffalo, Buffalo State University, Canisius University and D'Youville University all operate in the city.

The city adopted its Green Code in 2017, replacing zoning rules more than sixty years old. If you plan a change of use, such as turning a house into a different number of units, ask City Hall which code district applies before you spend money.

How does a Buffalo winter affect the value of a house?

Winters here are shaped by lake-effect snow bands coming off Lake Erie, in a humid continental climate. Wikipedia, citing Fox Weather, puts average snowfall near 95 inches a year and ranks Buffalo among the five snowiest large cities in the country.

Roofs, gutters, porches and plumbing absorb the abuse, so inspectors look at those first. If a worn roof is beyond your budget, an investor will fold the replacement into the price instead of asking you to do it.

What city rules apply if my Buffalo house is a rental?

Rental rules in the city affect how easily a tenant-occupied house changes hands, so read them before you list.

  • Every non-owner-occupied one- or two-family house must be on the Rental Registry, whether or not it is occupied. Some three-family and mixed-use buildings are covered as well.
  • A new registration costs $100. Since January 1, 2025 the yearly fee has been $50 for a single unit and $100 for a two-unit house.
  • Registered properties are scheduled for proactive inspection and must hold a Certificate of Rental Compliance. A property that fails cannot operate as an income property, and the tenants cannot be evicted for unpaid rent.
  • Landlords certify that a house built before 1978 may contain lead hazards, and the city will refuse a Certificate of Occupancy where lead paint is a hazard.
  • The city's Lead Hazard Reduction Grant offers up to $12,000 per unit in the Upper West Side and Schiller Park neighborhoods.

Short-term rentals need a separate license. A stay under six months qualifies, every address needs its own license, renewal is yearly, and a new owner has to apply from the start. Non-owner-occupied properties also need a special use permit. The Rental Registration office is at 65 Niagara Square, Room 304, phone 716-851-5621, and the short-term rental team answers at 716-851-4077.

What does closing cost in Erie County and who handles the deed?

Deeds for Buffalo houses are filed with the Erie County Clerk, whose posted charges are below.

  • $45 statutory recording fee plus $5 for each written page
  • $10 to file the TP-584 transfer tax form
  • $125 to file the RP-5217 transfer report on residential or farm property
  • Transfer tax of $4.50 per $500 of price, made up of $2.00 for New York State and $2.50 for Erie County, owed by the seller

At $160,000, that rate comes to $1,440. The clerk keeps the original deed on record and mails it back after the indexing is verified, and a Notice of Sale or Transfer of Ownership form accompanies a residential deed.

Inside the city, the Department of Assessment and Taxation reviews every deed filed to update ownership records. Its tax office sends delinquent notices, helps owners set up court-ordered payment plans and runs an annual In Rem foreclosure auction, so a house with unpaid city taxes is worth sorting out before an offer is signed. Ask that office for a current balance, including sewer rent, before you close, so no unpaid charge surprises you at the table.

More questions about Buffalo, NY

What if tenants still live in my Buffalo house?

A sale can go ahead with tenants in place. Ask the Rental Registration office whether your address holds a current Certificate of Rental Compliance, since the city says a rental that fails inspection cannot operate as an income property.

What does registering a Buffalo rental cost?

The first application costs $100. After that the yearly fee is $50 for one unit or $100 for two units, and LLCs or corporations owning rentals must also supply owner details at renewal.

Which side owes New York transfer tax on a Buffalo closing?

The seller does. Erie County's clerk posts a combined rate of $4.50 for each $500 of price: $2.00 to the state and $2.50 to the county. At $160,000 the bill is $1,440.

Is a permit required for nightly stays at a Buffalo house?

A Short-Term Rental License is required for any stay under six months. The license stays with the owner, so a purchaser who wants to continue short-term renting has to file a new application.

Which office files a Buffalo deed?

The Erie County Clerk's Office. The deed is signed and notarized, then filed together with Form TP-584 and the RP-5217 report, and the clerk returns the original by mail once it is recorded.

What are the quick ways to sell a North Hempstead house?

Owners in North Hempstead choose between a listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale and a direct cash purchase, and the right pick depends on how much work the house needs and how soon you must close. The first thing to settle is which government actually covers your address, because this town of about 239,000 people contains 31 incorporated villages.

North Hempstead is one of three towns in Nassau County, on Long Island, and Manhasset is the town seat. It covers 69.2 square miles, of which 15.7 are water, along Long Island Sound, Manhasset Bay, Hempstead Harbor and Little Neck Bay. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 238,982 people.

  • Typical home value among owners (2020 to 2024 median): $888,000
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 79.5%
  • Median gross rent: $2,318 a month
  • Median household income: $158,158
  • Mean commute to work: 35.5 minutes

At those values a sale carries real money at stake in repairs, carrying costs and tax proration, so it pays to compare a listing's net proceeds with a firm cash figure before you decide.

Which government covers my North Hempstead house, the town or a village?

When a house stands inside one of the 31 villages, the village sets its own zoning, and the town covers only the unincorporated hamlets. The town's Department of Building, Safety, Inspection and Enforcement says it administers State and Town codes in the unincorporated areas.

Wikipedia lists the villages, which include Great Neck, Roslyn, Westbury, Mineola, Williston Park, Lake Success, Sands Point and Kings Point, and the town-governed hamlets, which include Manhasset, Port Washington, Roslyn Heights, Carle Place, New Cassel, Albertson, Herricks and Searingtown. Check your tax bill or ask the town which applies before you ask for permit records, because a village house needs the village hall.

For hamlet properties, the town's Inspection Section issues building, plumbing and rental permits, and the Enforcement Section investigates construction and illegal housing complaints. Permit applications and records go through the town's online portal. The building department's phone number on the Receiver of Taxes page is (516) 869-6311. An open permit or an illegal conversion is the kind of problem that stalls a conventional sale, so look for them early.

How do North Hempstead property taxes work at a closing?

North Hempstead has two tax levies with different years, so the split at closing depends on the closing date. The Receiver of Taxes publishes a closing guide for attorneys and title companies that explains the periods.

Levy periods in North Hempstead (Town Receiver of Taxes closing information)

General, first halfJanuary 1 to June 30
General, second halfJuly 1 to December 31

School levies follow a July to June year, while general levies follow the calendar year. Incorporated villages bill their own taxes and may use assessed values that differ from the county roll, so a village owner has a third bill to settle. The Nassau County Department of Assessment manages assessments, and improvements made before a sale, including unreported work, can lift the assessed value beyond the 6% cap.

Two details catch sellers by surprise. Exemptions generally do not pass to the buyer, so a buyer must apply for their own. Nassau County can also add prorated restored taxes to a future bill when an exemption is removed after a sale, and that can take up to two years to appear.

How did North Hempstead take its shape?

North Hempstead was part of the Town of Hempstead until 1784, when it split off, and it takes its name from its position north of Hempstead. European settlement began around 1643, and the Matinecock Nation lived on the land before that. The town borders Queens on the west, Long Island Sound to the north, with Bronx County and Westchester County across the water, the Town of Oyster Bay and the City of Glen Cove to the east and the Town of Hempstead to the south.

The 31 villages claimed the right to set their own zoning, and no new village has formed in the town since Port Washington North in May 1932. The result is a patchwork where two houses a block apart can answer to different building departments. Unincorporated hamlets such as Manhasset, Port Washington, Roslyn Heights and Carle Place report directly to the town.

Which school districts serve North Hempstead?

The town splits across many districts, so the district code on your bill is the fact to check. The Receiver of Taxes lists codes for Westbury, East Williston, Roslyn, Port Washington, New Hyde Park, Manhasset, Great Neck, Herricks, Mineola, Carle Place, Floral Park, Glenwood Landing and Jericho.

The town has no say over residency disputes, which go to the school district or the State Education Department. Census figures show 60.7% of adults over 25 hold a four-year degree or more, and 92.7% finished high school.

What does a house sale cost in recording and transfer tax?

The seller pays New York's base transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price on a conveyance outside New York City, and the TP-584 return is filed with the county clerk where the property sits. For North Hempstead that is the Nassau County Clerk, whose number on the Receiver of Taxes page is (516) 571-2664.

The state also applies an additional one percent buyer-paid tax on residences priced at $1 million or more. That matters here because the median owner-occupied value is $888,000, so sales near the $1 million line are a live question for sellers and their buyers. The TP-584 and any tax are due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered.

If an LLC owns the house or will buy it, tell your attorney early. The state requires names and addresses of members, managers and other authorized persons when an LLC is on either side of a transfer of a building with up to four dwelling units.

What is the North Hempstead climate and housing stock like?

The town's climate is humid subtropical, close to the humid continental boundary, with hot, humid summers, cold winters and precipitation all year. Manhasset averages about 45 inches of precipitation and 23 inches of snow annually.

The town grew richer after the Long Island Rail Road reached Great Neck and steamboat service from Manhattan began in 1836. Its population rose from 26,370 in 1920 to 62,202 in 1930, 142,613 in 1950 and 219,088 in 1960, and it stood at 237,639 in 2020. Since most of that growth landed between 1930 and 1960, check the year built on your tax record and gather any permit paperwork for later additions before you list or take an offer.

  • Foreign-born residents, 2020 to 2024: 28.2%
  • People age 5 and older who speak a language other than English at home: 38.1%
  • Persons under 18: 22.6%
  • Persons 65 and older: 19.6%

More questions about North Hempstead, NY

Does the town or the village issue permits for my North Hempstead house?

That depends on the address. The town covers unincorporated hamlets such as Manhasset and Port Washington, and each of the 31 incorporated villages handles its own zoning. Check your tax bill or call the town if you are unsure.

Which office collects the tax bill for a North Hempstead house?

The Town Receiver of Taxes collects the town's general and school taxes, and incorporated villages collect their own village taxes. Nassau County's Department of Assessment sets the assessment.

Do exemptions like STAR carry over to the buyer?

Generally no. The buyer applies for their own exemptions through the Nassau County Department of Assessment, and a buyer who purchased after January 2, 2015 may be eligible for the STAR Credit program.

Who records the deed in North Hempstead?

The Nassau County Clerk records it. The seller pays the state transfer tax of $2 per $500, and the TP-584 is due within 15 days of the deed delivery.

How do I find my school district code?

Look it up on your tax bill or in the County Assessor's property search. The town lists codes from 001 for Westbury to 315 for Jericho, and residency disputes go to the district.

Where is the Town of Babylon, and which villages and hamlets are inside it?

One of Suffolk County's ten towns, Babylon fronts the Atlantic on Long Island's south shore. Nassau County is its western neighbor, Huntington lies north and Islip lies east. The western boundary sits roughly 20 miles from the Queens line.

Three incorporated villages and a long list of hamlets share the town, so an address can follow different local rules than the town name suggests.

  • Villages: Amityville in the southwest, Lindenhurst in the south and Babylon in the southeast
  • Hamlets: Copiague, Deer Park, East Farmingdale, North Amityville, North Babylon, North Lindenhurst, West Babylon, Wheatley Heights and Wyandanch
  • Barrier-island communities: Gilgo, Oak Beach, Captree and part of Fire Island west of the Robert Moses Causeway

Town Hall stands on East Sunrise Highway in Lindenhurst. For a house inside one of the villages, ask the village office what it adds on top of the town's taxes and permits.

How did Babylon grow into a town of 219,766 people?

The area was once called Huntington South. Around 1803 the families who settled there named it New Babylon, and in 1872 it became its own town, divided from Huntington.

The postwar decades were the big ones. Census counts went from 45,556 in 1950 to 142,309 in 1960 and 204,256 in 1970. Babylon has stayed above 200,000 since and reached 218,223 in 2020. Houses from that boom are decades old now, so a buyer will ask how old the roof and heating system are.

Know whether your address is in a village or a hamlet, because buyers compare areas closely.

How expensive is housing in Babylon by Census measures?

Owners live in 78.3% of Babylon's homes, and a typical owned home is valued at $522,100. Owners with a mortgage report monthly costs near $3,206.

Households average 3.13 people, well above the national 2.53, and 93.5% of residents had the same address a year earlier. With owner costs that high, the tax bill gets close attention from buyers.

How do the railroad and airports shape Babylon buyers' choices?

The Long Island Rail Road's Babylon Branch is the principal line, with stops from Amityville to Babylon village. The Main Line passes through the northern hamlets, serving Pinelawn, Wyandanch and Deer Park. Suffolk County Transit buses cover most of the rest.

Republic Airport in East Farmingdale houses the American Airpower Museum, and Long Island MacArthur Airport in Ronkonkoma, nearby, has commercial flights. Workers here average a 31.0 minute commute, against 26.4 nationally.

Distance to a station is worth stating. Say which station is closest when you describe the house.

What does the Great South Bay shoreline mean for a Babylon house?

Water makes up over half of the town's 114 square miles, and its elevation averages about 6.6 feet. The Great South Bay, Fire Island Inlet and Atlantic beaches form the southern line. Town parks include Southard's Pond Park in the village and Tanner Park in Copiague, and state parks include Belmont Lake, Captree and Robert Moses.

Low ground and open water shape insurance, repairs and buyer questions. Ask your insurance agent whether your house sits in a flood zone before you list.

Sewer billing shifted in 2026. On January 1 all Suffolk County sewer districts merged into the Suffolk County Wastewater Management District, which may have changed your rate or billing method. Check the sewer line on your tax bill.

What is the Babylon tax calendar, and what do late payments cost?

Babylon's tax year starts December 1 and ends November 30, with one bill mailed around mid-December. An owner may pay it whole or in halves. For 2025-26, the first half fell due in the second week of January 2026 and the second half at the end of May, and both have passed. The next bill is due to arrive in mid-December.

  • A first half paid late grows by 1% for each month, topping out at 5% in mid to late May.
  • Once May ends, unpaid taxes are delinquent and go to the Suffolk County Comptroller in Riverhead, with a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest running from February 1.
  • The office takes partial payments starting at $200.
  • Cards online add a 2.35% fee and e-checks add $1.
  • If a balance is still open at the tax lien sale, usually in December, the county sells a lien on the property.

The Receiver of Taxes collects but does not set rates. School, county and town budgets decide the amounts, and school tax is usually the biggest line. A missing bill is no excuse for a late payment.

How can a Babylon owner pay a tax bill, and who else can receive a copy?

Taxes can be paid online through the payment processor, by mail with a detached stub, or at Town Hall in the main hallway. In person, the office takes cash and checks but not cards, and a drop box accepts checks during business hours. Mailed payments are credited on the postmark date, and a metered postmark does not count.

An owner who is 65 or older, or disabled, and who lives in a one, two or three-family home may name a consenting adult to receive duplicate bills and notices of unpaid taxes. That application is due by October 1. For a parent's house you are about to sell, it is worth asking whether such a notice was ever set up.

Which exemptions and assessment deadlines affect a Babylon sale?

Babylon's Department of Assessment takes exemption applications until March 1 and denies late ones. The list includes Enhanced STAR, Aged, Alternative Veterans, Cold War Veterans, volunteer firefighter and ambulance worker, disability with limited income, Capital Improvement and first-time buyer of a newly built home. Newcomers to Basic STAR get a state credit in place of a school tax exemption.

One point matters at sale: an exemption follows the person who qualified. If your house carries a senior or veteran exemption, the buyer should expect it to end, and the tax bill could climb. Tell the buyer early.

Complaints about an assessment use Form RP-524. Suffolk County's town review boards sit on the third Tuesday in May, which is May 18 in 2027. The town builds values from square footage and amenities.

What happens at a Babylon closing, and where does a cash offer fit?

New York's transfer tax, two dollars for each $500 of price, is normally the seller's expense. The Suffolk County Clerk files the TP-584 return, and payment is due 15 days after the deed is delivered.

Third-party payers such as banks, title companies and attorneys pay a $1 duplicate tax bill fee, sent as a separate check. Plan for that when a title company clears your open tax bill at closing.

A listed sale follows the buyer's mortgage schedule. A cash purchase takes the house as it is and can close on your timeline, which suits deferred repairs, an overdue tax balance or an estate. In both cases, line up the deed, the latest tax statement and a lender payoff.

More questions about Babylon, NY

When do Babylon tax payments come due?

Bills mail in mid-December. Half is due in the second week of January and half at the end of May, and a late first half gains 1% a month.

Where do Babylon taxes go after May 31?

They go to the Suffolk County Comptroller's Office in Riverhead, carrying a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest counted from February 1.

Does my STAR or senior exemption pass to the buyer in Babylon?

No. A new owner applies separately, and the tax bill may rise. The application deadline is March 1.

Do Babylon sellers owe a transfer tax?

Yes, the state charges two dollars per $500 of price, usually paid by the seller, with the TP-584 filed at the Suffolk County Clerk 15 days after the deed.

When must a Babylon assessment complaint be filed?

Suffolk County's town boards meet on the third Tuesday in May. The form is RP-524, and filing costs nothing.

  • Williamsville, the incorporated village in the south
  • Getzville and the Audubon area, near the center
  • East Amherst and Swormville, shared with the Town of Clarence
  • North Bailey, around Bailey Avenue and Maple Road

Mailing addresses can cross town lines. Some homes east of Transit Road carry a Williamsville address yet belong to the Town of Clarence for taxes and schools, so read the tax bill to see which municipality applies.

What turned Amherst from farmland into a suburb?

The state carved Amherst out of the Town of Buffalo on April 10, 1818. After the Erie Canal opened in 1825, German farmers took up the northern land and mills went up along Ellicott Creek. Williamsville began in the 1810s, Eggertsville and Snyder in the 1830s, East Amherst and Swormville in the 1850s and Getzville in the 1860s.

The real surge came after World War II. Census counts read 13,181 in 1930, 31,407 in 1950, 90,734 in 1970 and 129,595 in 2020. Nearly tripling in twenty years suggests many of today's subdivisions date to that stretch.

A house that age may need work on kitchens, baths and mechanical systems. A financed buyer may negotiate repairs, and a cash buyer will usually fold them into the price.

How do Amherst's housing numbers compare with the rest of New York?

Owners live in 69.9% of Amherst homes, and the Census Bureau puts a typical owned home at $311,600.

Over one resident in five is 65 or older, and 86.4% were at the same address a year earlier. Long tenure like that often ends in a downsize or an estate sale.

Which school district is a house in, and what colleges are nearby?

Four public districts divide the town. Williamsville Central is the biggest, taking the eastern half and some of Clarence. Amherst Central has the southwest, around Eggertsville and Snyder, with Amherst Central High School. Sweet Home Central has the northwest, including West Amherst and Getzville, and Clarence Central has a small southeastern corner.

Colleges add renters and buyers. The University at Buffalo's North Campus lies here, along with Daemen University, an Erie Community College campus and a Bryant and Stratton College campus.

Name the district whenever you describe the house. Two homes sharing a ZIP code can fall in different districts.

What roads and weather should an Amherst seller keep in mind?

The Thruway (I-90) crosses the south end. I-290 cuts diagonally toward Tonawanda, and I-990, the Lockport Expressway, lies wholly inside Amherst and ends at Millersport Highway.

Surface routes tie the hamlets together. US 62 marks the west line as Niagara Falls Boulevard, then carries on as Sheridan Drive and Bailey Avenue. Main Street is Route 5, Transit Road (Route 78) is the east line, and Harlem Road, Campbell Boulevard and Sheridan Drive are Routes 240, 270 and 324.

Average highs span 31 to 47 degrees from November to March and 60 to 81 from May to October, so a long cold season makes roof, gutter and furnace condition easy to notice during a showing.

What do Amherst's rental rules mean if tenants live in the house?

Chapter 44 of the town code bars renting a unit until the owner holds a rental registration certificate. An owner-occupied property with two or fewer units, if not used for short stays, is exempt.

  • The standard certificate lasts up to three years, with a $75 inspection fee for each unit.
  • Stays of 1 to 30 days count as short-term rentals. Those certificates last one year, come with an annual inspection, and cost $250 a unit if the owner lives there or $500 if not, per the 2025 form.
  • No certificate issues until the unit passes inspection and local property taxes are current.
  • Owners living outside Erie, Niagara and Genesee counties need a local agent.
  • Houses built before 1978 carry a lead paint certification on the form.

A buyer can take over a certificate's remaining term by filing a transfer application with the Commissioner of Building within 30 days of the deed. Skipping registration can double the fee, add a $75 fine and lead to a notice to vacate, and a code violation can bring up to $1,500 or 15 days in jail.

How do assessment complaints and county tax liens work in Amherst?

The town Assessor values each parcel, and an owner who disagrees files RP-524. Most communities use the fourth Tuesday in May as the cutoff, which would be May 25 in 2027, so confirm it with the Assessor's Office at 5583 Main Street in Williamsville. That office has taken paperwork by mail or drop-off as well as hearings in person.

Erie County may foreclose liens that sit unpaid for two years or longer. The In Rem 173 action started September 9, 2025 for 2022 and earlier liens, with November 10, 2025 as the final redemption date. To redeem, an owner paid the back taxes and a $500 statutory fee by cash, certified check, bank check or money order to the County Director of Real Property Tax Services. Parcels not redeemed head to public auction, and later years' taxes continue to accrue.

If back taxes are owed, request a payoff figure from Erie County Real Property Tax Services, since the balance grows with fees and interest. Closing proceeds can retire a lien, so have the title company order the figure early.

What will the state tax cost on an Amherst sale, and which sale routes exist?

The state taxes a conveyance at two dollars per $500 of price, a cost that usually falls on the seller. The Erie County Clerk takes the TP-584 return, due 15 days after the deed changes hands.

Owners can hire an agent, sell without one or accept a cash offer. An agent sale involves showings and a closing date set by the buyer's lender. A cash buyer takes the house in its current condition, which suits a rental near the end of its certificate, an inherited house or a parcel with back taxes.

Whichever you pick, locate the deed, the latest town and school tax bills, any rental certificate and your lender's payoff statement.

More questions about Amherst, NY

Does a tenant-occupied Amherst house need a rental certificate at sale?

Registration is the owner's duty while the unit is rented. A buyer can take it over by filing within 30 days of the deed, so hand over the certificate and inspection paperwork.

What is the cutoff for contesting an Amherst assessment?

Most New York communities use the fourth Tuesday in May. Check the exact day with the Amherst Assessor's Office. The form is RP-524, and there is no charge to file.

What happens when county tax liens stay unpaid on an Amherst property?

Erie County can foreclose once liens are two or more years old. Owners receive notice and a last redemption date, with a $500 fee, and anything left unredeemed goes to public auction.

What would the state transfer tax be on a typical Amherst sale?

At two dollars per $500, a sale at the Census value of $311,600 owes about $1,248, since each partial $500 counts as a full one.

How do I find which district my Amherst house belongs to?

It is one of Williamsville, Amherst, Sweet Home or Clarence Central, depending on location. The tax bill names it, and the Assessor's Office can confirm.

Where does Albany sit, and how does its shape affect a sale?

New York's capital is also Albany County's seat. It lies on the Hudson roughly 135 miles up the river from Manhattan, inside 21.8 square miles (21.4 of land), with Colonie to its north, Guilderland to its west and Bethlehem to its south.

The interior is rolling ground left from ancient Lake Albany, with sandy, dry soil under much of the western side. The highest natural point is a benchmark near the Loudonville Reservoir at 378 feet, and the lowest ground sits along the tidal Hudson. The Albany Pine Bush, a pine barrens preserve set up by the Legislature in 1988, hugs the west side and crosses into the neighboring towns.

People describe Albany as a city of neighborhoods, and buyers shop by neighborhood first. A few of the best known:

  • Arbor Hill, including the Ten Broeck Triangle rowhouses
  • Center Square, a mix of homes, restaurants and shops
  • Pine Hills, on the city's western side
  • The South End, by the river

What do Census numbers show about Albany homes and renters?

Renters outnumber owners in Albany. Owners live in just 38.2% of homes, and a typical owned home is worth $234,700. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 count of 101,698 people is 2.6% above its 2020 base.

Owners with a mortgage pay about $1,847 a month, while the typical renter pays $1,216. If your building has tenants, buyers will ask about leases and inspection certificates early.

What jobs keep Albany's housing demand steady?

Government, health care, education and a growing technology sector carry the local economy, and that mix has historically cushioned it from national recessions. More than 162,000 people are in the city on a typical weekday, well above the resident count.

Campuses bring in students and staff who rent. The University at Albany, Albany Medical College, Albany Law School and the College of Saint Rose are among the schools in or near the city, and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and SUNY Polytechnic anchor the region's nanotechnology work.

Since the 2010s a cluster of video game developers has also grown in and around the city. For an owner of a small rental near a campus or downtown, those payrolls are the reason tenants keep coming, and they give a buyer a story to underwrite.

What do Albany's snowy winters do to an older house?

A typical Albany year brings 40.7 inches of precipitation and 59.4 inches of snow. Expect around nine nights at zero or colder and around nine days at 90 or hotter.

Swings like that are hard on older buildings, and inspectors look at the same few spots.

  • Roof condition and ice damming along eaves after heavy snow
  • Pipes in unheated spaces, since cold snaps below zero repeat each winter
  • Basement and foundation condition after repeated freeze and thaw
  • Heating systems in houses built before central air, where summer humidity is now a comfort issue

A cash buyer prices repairs into the offer. A buyer using a mortgage may send you a repair request after the inspection.

Which highways, rail stops and school districts matter to Albany buyers?

The Thruway is the main artery, signed as I-90 heading west and I-87 heading south. I-787 connects downtown to it and continues north to Troy and Watervliet, while an untolled stretch of I-90 wraps the north and east.

Passenger trains stop at the Albany-Rensselaer station on the east bank, and the airport is in Colonie. CDTA buses run through the city to Schenectady, Troy and Saratoga Springs.

The City School District of Albany runs the public schools. Charter schools and private options such as Albany Academy and Bishop Maginn High School also operate here.

Which Albany registries can hold up a closing?

The city's Buildings and Regulatory Compliance department keeps several registries. When a registration expires, a hold goes on the property record and no permits issue until the lapse is fixed.

  • Vacant buildings: the rule dates to July 1, 2000. Register as soon as a building empties or when you buy an empty one, then renew yearly. A one to three unit house pays $250 for the first year, $500 for the second, $750 for the third and $1,000 for each year after. Not registering risks a penalty of up to $1,000 a day.
  • Rental units: inspection and certification come up every 24 months for $50 a unit.
  • Waste collection fee: new in 2026, it shows on the tax bill at $180 a unit, and unpaid balances move to the next bill with late charges.

Red placards on some empty buildings tell firefighters about structural hazards. If one of those is yours, ask the department where the registration stands before you take an offer.

When can you challenge an Albany assessment, and when do tax bills come due?

Complaints can be filed from May 1 until the fourth Tuesday in May, which fell on May 26 in 2026. The next window opens May 1, 2027, and the form is RP-524. There is no filing charge.

New construction, fires, demolitions and periodic citywide updates are what move an assessment. Exemption applications, Basic STAR included, are accepted January 1 through March 1, and all owners sign.

A city bill can be split. Half is due January 31 (February 6 for eligible seniors) and the rest is billed in July, with split payments limited to check or cash. Online payment covers only full amounts. Mailed payments count on the postmark, so skip bill-pay services that do not use one.

Before you close, have the title company check the city bill, the waste collection fee and school tax line by line.

What does an Albany sale cost in state tax, and where does a cash offer fit?

The state's transfer tax is two dollars per $500 of the sale price, usually the seller's cost. Albany County's clerk receives the TP-584 return and payment within 15 days of the deed.

Going through an agent means preparing the house, hosting showings and waiting on a buyer's lender. A cash purchase skips that and closes when you pick, a fit for an empty house, a lapsed rental certificate or an estate.

Either way, pull together the deed, the latest tax bill, registry certificates and your lender's payoff letter. If the house has tenants, add the leases and the most recent rental certificate so a buyer can see the inspection status at a glance.

More questions about Albany, NY

Can I sell a vacant house in Albany without fixing it first?

Yes. The city requires the vacant building registration to stay current, but it does not require repairs before a sale. A buyer who takes the house as-is inherits the registration duty, so confirm the annual fee is paid before closing.

When is Albany's grievance deadline?

The deadline is the fourth Tuesday in May, and the window opens May 1. In 2026 that day was May 26. Forms are available from the Assessor's Office at City Hall beginning May 1.

How much is the vacant building fee in Albany?

For a one to three unit residential building it is $250 in the first year, $500 in the second, $750 in the third and $1,000 for each later year. Larger and non-residential buildings pay more under the city's schedule.

Does the buyer or the seller pay New York's transfer tax?

The seller pays the base state transfer tax of $2 per $500, unless the contract says otherwise. The 1% mansion tax applies to residences of $1 million or more and is paid by the buyer.

What documents should an Albany seller have ready?

Bring the deed, the most recent city and school tax bills, proof that registry certificates are current, any rental registration or certificate of occupancy paperwork, and a mortgage payoff statement. If tenants live there, add leases and the rental dwelling certificate.

How does the village and town split affect a Greenburgh home sale?

Which offices handle your sale depends on whether the house is in one of the town's six villages or in the unincorporated area. Greenburgh lies in western Westchester County. The Hudson River forms its western edge, Yonkers lies south, Mount Pleasant north, and White Plains and Scarsdale to the east.

Wikipedia's entry on Greenburgh gives the founding year as 1788 and the land area as about 30 of its 36 square miles, with 95,397 people counted in 2020. About half of them live inside villages. The remainder live in unincorporated pockets such as the Fairview, Greenville and Hartsdale census areas, plus North Elmsford and South Ardsley.

The town Building Department says it takes complaints only for the unincorporated part of Greenburgh, and the Tax Department sends village residents to their own Village Hall for due dates. So a seller in Tarrytown has two sets of offices to check, while a seller in Hartsdale deals mainly with the town.

What do Census figures show about Greenburgh housing costs?

The Census Bureau's profile puts the median value of owner-occupied homes at $697,100 for 2020 to 2024, a level where closing costs and the state's one percent high-value threshold start to matter. The figures below come from that profile.

A commute of that length fits a town where rail service into the city is a main draw. At $2,316 a month, median rent is a useful yardstick if you are weighing a sale against keeping the house as a rental. About a quarter of residents were born abroad (24.3 percent), and 30.6 percent of people age five and over speak another language at home, so listing materials in more than one language can widen the audience.

Which trains, roads and schools do Greenburgh buyers ask about?

  • Trains: Metro-North's Hudson Line stops in Hastings-on-Hudson, Dobbs Ferry, Ardsley-on-Hudson, Irvington and Tarrytown. The Harlem Line has a Hartsdale station.
  • Highways: the Thruway, the Cross Westchester Expressway, and the Saw Mill River, Bronx River and Sprain Brook parkways all pass through, along with US 9 and state routes 9A, 100 and 119.
  • Buses: the county's Bee-Line system runs in town.
  • Schools: the tax office bills for ten separate school districts, so the district on your bill is the first thing most buyers check.

Since the district changes the total tax bill from one street to the next, pull your current bill before you set a price.

Which Greenburgh building rules should you check before listing?

The Building Department's FAQ says a permit is needed for any construction, repair, improvement, modification or demolition. A re-roof on a one or two family house counts, and structural roof changes need drawings sealed by a New York State architect or engineer.

  • Sheds of every size need a permit. The limit is one per lot, in the rear yard, at 150 square feet and 10 feet high at most.
  • A fence needs no building permit up to six feet in a front or side yard and eight feet in the rear, with a 30 inch cap near corners.
  • Repaving an existing driveway needs no permit, but enlarging it does, and Public Works may also require a curb cut or right-of-way permit.
  • Pulling or abandoning a heating oil tank takes its own permit and inspection.
  • No residential zoning district lists short-term rentals as a permitted use.

That last rule matters when a buyer plans a vacation rental. The department's forms page says applications are taken in person or by mail on weekdays at 177 Hillside Avenue, and it posts its current hours there.

How are Greenburgh property taxes collected and what happens at closing?

The Receiver of Taxes bills for the county, the town, the fire districts and ten school districts, a total the Tax Department page puts above a quarter billion dollars a year. It describes the office as the largest municipal collection agency in Westchester. The first installment of the 2026 school tax was due September 30, 2026, so that deadline is behind you. Get the next due date and a written balance from the office before closing.

  • Checks are payable to the Greenburgh Receiver of Taxes, 177 Hillside Avenue. Online card payments carry a variable fee, while ACH payments are free.
  • Liens cannot be paid online and must be settled at the Tax Office.
  • Last-day hours run to 7 p.m. on January 31, April 30 and September 30.
  • A new owner should call the tax office so future bills go to the right person.

Two state rules are quoted on the page. A bill that never arrives does not erase the tax or interest (Real Property Tax Law section 922), and the Receiver has no authority to waive a penalty (section 920). If you have moved out, send your new mailing address to the office in writing.

How does the Greenburgh assessment roll work?

The Assessment Rolls page says the tentative roll is open to the public by June 1. The Board of Assessment Review decides appeals until the roll becomes final on September 15, and that final roll is a snapshot that ignores later small claims changes. The page links the 2026 Final Assessment Roll as the current one.

Check your own line on the roll against what similar houses nearby sold for. A buyer's attorney will read the same record, and the Assessor's Office can answer questions about the latest figure.

What does the Westchester County Clerk need to record a Greenburgh deed?

Deeds go to the Land Records Division of the Westchester County Clerk. Its recording guide lists four required pieces: a cover page made in the county's PREP system, a TP-584, an RP-5217 transfer report, and a payment cover page showing fees and tax.

The clerk gives the state transfer tax as $2 per $500 of price, rounding up to the next $500, and its example turns a $404,501 price into $1,620. Using the same math, a sale at the $697,100 median would owe about $2,790. Separately, a house or condo for one to three families conveyed at $1,000,000 or more owes a one percent mansion tax. The clerk's staff do not draft deeds or advise on them, so lean on your attorney for the document.

What should a Greenburgh seller prepare first?

  • The property condition disclosure statement required by Real Property Law section 462, handed over before any binding contract is signed.
  • Certificates of occupancy or completion for any finished space, and permit records for recent work.
  • Town, county and school tax bills, plus a village bill if you live in a village.
  • A lender payoff letter and details of any lien.
  • Your STAR status: the state asks owners to close a registration after a sale.

More questions about Greenburgh, NY

Do village homes in Greenburgh use the town Building Department?

Generally not. The town department says it handles complaints in the unincorporated part of Greenburgh only. For a house in a village such as Tarrytown, ask the village hall about permits and due dates.

Is a permit needed for a new roof in Greenburgh?

Yes. A roof covering replacement on a one or two family house needs a building permit with drawings, and any structural change needs plans from a licensed architect or engineer.

Can the next owner run a short-term rental from a Greenburgh house?

The town says short-term rentals are not a permitted use in any residential zoning district. A buyer with that plan should confirm with the Building Department before closing.

What transfer tax applies to a $700,000 Greenburgh sale?

State tax is $2 for every $500, which comes to $2,800 on $700,000. The one percent mansion tax starts at $1,000,000 for one to three family homes and condos.

Where do Greenburgh property tax payments go?

They go to the Greenburgh Receiver of Taxes at 177 Hillside Avenue, which collects for the county, town, fire districts and ten school districts. Village residents follow their village's own schedule.

What is it like to sell a house in Greece, New York?

Greece is the largest town in Monroe County by population and sits directly northwest of Rochester, so a seller here competes with a deep supply of suburban houses. It was established on March 22, 1822, and it reaches from Ridge Road in the south to the Lake Ontario shoreline in the north.

The Rochester suburb is bordered by the city on the east, the town of Gates on the south, and the towns of Parma and Ogden on the west. According to Wikipedia's article on Greece, the town covers about 51 square miles, roughly 47.5 of them land. Wetlands and ponds, including Braddock Bay, line the northern edge near the lake. The disclosure form asks about wetlands and flood zones, so answer those lines from the lake side of town with care.

Ridge Road, which is NY-104, follows an old glacial lakeshore and carries most of the shopping. NY-18 (Latta Road) runs through North Greece, the Lake Ontario State Parkway crosses the northern part of town, and I-390 runs north and south through the east side. The same article records the town growing from about 25,500 people in 1950 to about 75,100 in 1970, and it notes that thousands of residents drove the Ridge to Kodak jobs in the 1940s.

Which schools serve Greece and why does it matter to a seller?

Three districts serve the town: Greece Central, Hilton Central and Spencerport Central. Greece Central is by far the largest, with roughly 11,000 students, and it is the seventh largest district in New York State outside New York City. Its secondary schools are Arcadia, Athena, Olympia and Odyssey, with the Phoenix Academy for grades 7 to 12.

Put the district name in your listing or your message to a cash buyer. The state's disclosure form has a line for the school district, and the town's ZIP codes include 14468 for Hilton and 14559 for Spencerport, so a mailing address alone does not tell you which district applies.

Which Greece town rules can slow down a sale?

Open permits and exterior code violations are the two items that most often delay a closing. The Town of Greece Building Department, part of Technical Services at One Vince Tofany Boulevard, requires a permit for remodels and additions to a single-family house, and it requires professionally prepared plans when the work costs more than $20,000.

  • Inspection stages for a permitted job run from footing and foundation through rough framing, insulation, final grading and an electrical sign-off by one of three listed inspection agencies, then a final town inspection.
  • The town's property maintenance law covers vacant land and buildings as well as occupied homes. It sets fines of up to $1,000 or a year in jail per violation, and the town can fix a problem and add the bill to the property tax bill.
  • Every residential property must have active refuse service, and unlicensed or dismantled vehicles may not be stored outdoors.
  • Real estate signs are limited to one sign of six square feet or less, and they cannot go in the right of way or on utility poles.

The permit applications page also lists short-term and long-term rental applications next to the building forms, which matters if the house is a rental you plan to hand over with tenants in place.

How are Greece property taxes billed and collected?

The Receiver of Taxes collects town general taxes in January for the calendar year. The tax collection page says bills are mailed in early January and combine levies for the Town, Monroe County, the Greece Fire District, the Greece Central School District and any special districts. Unpaid school or water bills are re-levied onto this general bill, so ask the closing attorney to check for them.

The town does not set the county, fire district or school rates. It collects on their behalf. You can pay in person at Town Hall on weekdays or use the 24 hour drop at the Service Mall entrance. Online payment goes through the Monroe County website and carries a 3 percent card charge, and the office does not accept payment by phone.

How can a Greece owner contest an assessment before selling?

Greece offers a three step path, and the first step is free and early. The Assessor's page describes it this way.

  • Informal hearing: held from January to March by appointment with the Assessor's Office.
  • Board of Assessment Review: file form RP-524 after May 1 and no later than the fourth Tuesday of May, and ask for a hearing or a paper review.
  • Judicial review: if the board result still looks wrong, form RPTL-730 must be filed with fees within 30 days of final roll publication.

The page says Greece assesses property as of March 1, using the preceding July 1 as the valuation day, and that the office maintains about 34,500 property records and processes roughly 25,000 exemptions. A lower assessment helps a buyer, so a successful challenge before listing can support a better price.

What does recording a deed cost in Monroe County?

Greece deeds are filed with the Monroe County Clerk at 39 West Main Street in Rochester. The clerk's land records page lists the current charges, and you must be in line by 4:30 p.m. to record the same day.

  • One page deed: $50, plus $5 for each additional page.
  • TP-584 form: $5.
  • Equalization form RP-5217: $125 for the common residential cases, otherwise $250.
  • Transfer tax: $4 per thousand dollars of price.
  • An added $10 fee applies to each residential deed.

On a $190,000 house the transfer tax line would be $760 and the fixed fees would add roughly $190, so figure about $950 before any attorney charge. Your attorney will confirm the final figure.

What should a Greece seller line up before offers arrive?

  • The signed property condition disclosure statement required by Real Property Law section 462, in the buyer's hands ahead of a signed contract.
  • Permit records for any finished basement, deck, pool or addition.
  • A recent tax bill, so the attorney can see the Town, Monroe County, fire district and school lines.
  • Mortgage payoff information and a list of any liens.
  • Keys, access and a target closing date.

More questions about Greece, NY

Is Greece, NY part of Rochester?

No. Greece is a separate town in Monroe County, and Rochester is the city on its eastern border. A house in Greece is taxed by the Town of Greece, the county and the fire district, and it is served by Greece Central, Hilton Central or Spencerport Central schools.

Do I need a permit record to sell a Greece house?

The town does not issue a sale permit, but open building permits and exterior code violations can hold up a closing. Ask the Building Department to confirm any past work was closed out.

When do Greece town and county taxes get billed?

Bills are mailed in early January and cover January 1 through December 31. The Receiver of Taxes collects them, and an unpaid school or water bill is moved onto the general tax bill.

How much is the Monroe County transfer tax on a deed?

The clerk lists transfer tax at $4 per thousand dollars of the sale price. A $200,000 sale would carry $800 of that tax, in addition to the recording and form fees.

What is the deadline to grieve a Greece assessment?

Form RP-524 is filed after May 1 and no later than the fourth Tuesday of May. Informal hearings with the Assessor run earlier, from January to March.

Where is Clarkstown, NY, and what does the town include?

Clarkstown is the most densely populated town in Rockland County, on the county's eastern edge with the Hudson River as its boundary. The town was created on March 18, 1791 out of Haverstraw. It covers about 47 square miles, of which roughly 38.5 are land and 8.6 are water, and the 2020 census counted 86,855 residents.

The hamlet of New City is the county seat and also the seat of town government, the Clarkstown Police Department, the county sheriff's office and the county correctional facility. New City accounts for about 41 percent of the town's population. The town also holds Bardonia, Congers, Central Nyack, Nanuet, Valley Cottage, West Nyack, Rockland Lake, Mount Ivy, the village of Upper Nyack, and the eastern part of the village of Spring Valley.

Four state parks lie inside the town: High Tor, Hook Mountain, Nyack Beach and Rockland Lake, along with Lake DeForest and Lake Lucille. The Palisades Center is of the largest malls in the world, and Clarkstown has more business districts than any other town in the county.

  • The New York State Thruway (I-87 and I-287) crosses the Palisades Interstate Parkway inside the town.
  • Clarkstown Mini-Trans runs five local bus routes.
  • NJ Transit's Pascack Valley Line stops at Nanuet, and Rockland Coaches runs express service to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Which school districts serve Clarkstown houses?

Several districts divide the town, so the address matters. The Clarkstown Central School District serves most of it, including New City, Bardonia, Congers and West Nyack. Nyack Public Schools serve Upper Nyack, Valley Cottage and Central Nyack, the Nanuet Union Free School District serves Nanuet, and a small slice on the western border belongs to East Ramapo.

High schools inside the town are Clarkstown North in New City, Clarkstown South in West Nyack, Nyack Senior High in Upper Nyack and Nanuet Senior High in Nanuet. Quote the district from the tax bill, since one street can sit in a different district from the next.

When are Clarkstown property taxes due, and what do they cover?

Clarkstown's Town Clerk, at 10 Maple Avenue in New City, collects town and county property tax for a calendar year. Full payment is due by January 31 with no penalty. The town's calendar lists the late fees and the quarterly option below.

Payment choiceDate or windowCharge
Full payment, no penaltyBy January 31None
Full paymentFebruary 1 to 28Additional 1%
Full paymentMarch 1 to 31Additional 2%
Quarterly paymentsJanuary 15, April 15, July 15, October 155% service charge
